Chapter 2: The Power of Sampling and Learning from Many Fields
Picture this for a second—a teenager who spends their afternoons jumping from one hobby to another. Maybe they're playing soccer in the fall, joining the school play in the winter, dabbling in coding come spring, and then picking up a guitar for the summer. To some folks, that might look like they can’t make up their mind, or maybe they just can't stick to one thing. But for that young person? Every new experience brings in a fresh perspective, a new skill, and a growing sense of what truly fits.
This idea, often brushed off as just “sampling,” is actually a powerful way to learn. Instead of locking yourself into one path from the start, sampling lets you build a toolkit packed with all sorts of skills and experiences. You learn how to learn, how to adapt, and how to spot connections that others just don’t see.
Let’s look at sports for a minute. Incredibly, many top athletes didn’t stick to just one sport early on. They played all kinds of games, building a broad base of both physical and mental abilities. So when they finally chose to specialize, they brought all those different strengths with them. Their bodies were more resilient, their minds more flexible, and they came up with creative ways to train that most people never would have tried.
And it’s not just sports. The same thing shows up in science. Some of the most innovative thinkers started out in one field, then jumped to another—bringing fresh ideas and new methods with them. In business, leaders who’ve worked in several industries often spot opportunities that others just miss. Being able to take knowledge from one area, recognize patterns, make analogies, and connect the dots—that’s what sets generalists apart.
But here’s something to pay attention to: it’s not just about having lots of interests. It’s about how you learn. When you sample widely, you’re forced to tackle problems from different angles. You get comfortable with ambiguity, you learn to ask better questions, and you’re okay with not knowing all the answers right away. Sure, this kind of learning can feel slower at the start, but in the long run, it pays off in big ways.
There’s a great story about a young scientist who started out in engineering, switched to biology, and eventually found their way into medicine. Every step brought new challenges, but also new ways of thinking. So when a complex problem came up, they didn’t just rely on one set of tools—they pulled from everything they’d learned, combining ideas in ways that pure specialists might never even consider.
Most people don’t realize just how valuable this kind of experience really is. There’s a lot of pressure to pick one thing early and stick with it, and folks who wander a bit are often seen as unfocused. But here’s the truth: sampling widely isn’t a weakness—it’s a real strength. The world is full of problems that don’t fit neatly into one box, and it’s the people who can draw from lots of different experiences who usually come up with the best solutions.
So here’s the key takeaway: learning isn’t just about going deep, it’s about going wide, too. The more fields you explore, the more tools you have when you need them, and the more likely you are to stumble onto something new and valuable. The path might look winding, but it leads to places a straight line never could.
